STEP 3.5-1. COMPETITIVE RESPONSE SIMULATION
ADSK's stated differentiation is "project intelligence" — using design, build and operations
data to train models that make Autodesk software faster and smarter. If this SUCCEEDS, the
response is asymmetric and unfavourable: AI lowers the barrier to entry in entry-level CAD
and in simple drafting. The incumbent's moat is file-format inertia and trained users, both
of which are weak against a generative tool that reads a drawing and emits a model. Dassault,
Bentley and Nemetschek respond in the enterprise tier; AI-native entrants attack the bottom.
Net second-order impact: **−2 of +3.** ADSK's historical defence — that nobody re-does a
building in a new file format — does not protect the FIRST draft.

STEP 3.5-2. REFLEXIVITY CHECK (Soros)
Negative loop (active and self-reinforcing): a lower share price makes SBC-denominated
compensation less attractive to engineers competing with AI labs for the same talent, while
the CFO has already committed to REDUCING SBC to 9% of revenue. A depressed stock also
removes equity as M&A currency — which is why ADSK paid CASH for MaintainX, and cash is
what the balance sheet has least of. Positive loop: a high multiple historically let ADSK
attract talent and acquire cheaply. That loop is currently UNWINDING, not compounding.
Net: **−1.** I do not treat this as decisive, but it argues against the reflexive bull case.

STEP 3.5-3. CUSTOMER BEHAVIOUR EVOLUTION
ADSK is deliberately moving from seat-based to consumptive models (Flex, token-based) and
from task-based to workflow- and systems-level automation [Actual — CEO, Q2 FY27 call].
Management states AI is gross-profit-dollar accretive but causes SLIGHT GROSS MARGIN
COMPRESSION, and says this is already in the 41% FY29 operating-margin target [Actual — CFO].
The second-order risk: consumptive pricing shifts revenue recognition later and makes the
revenue line lumpier — which interacts badly with a market that is currently rewarding
visible billings. Early-adopter → mainstream transition in AEC is slow (multi-year
procurement cycles), which caps how fast any of this shows up in FY28.
